Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.

Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("03bbc4fa1fd784276da135ab62fef85aaddea66e6eb176d7e59c3398f818b153") or SHA1 in~ ("03bbc4fa1fd784276da135ab62fef85aaddea66e6eb176d7e59c3398f818b153") or MD5 in~ ("03bbc4fa1fd784276da135ab62fef85aaddea66e6eb176d7e59c3398f818b153")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("03bbc4fa1fd784276da135ab62fef85aaddea66e6eb176d7e59c3398f818b153") or SHA1 in~ ("03bbc4fa1fd784276da135ab62fef85aaddea66e6eb176d7e59c3398f818b153") or MD5 in~ ("03bbc4fa1fd784276da135ab62fef85aaddea66e6eb176d7e59c3398f818b153")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["03bbc4fa1fd784276da135ab62fef85aaddea66e6eb176d7e59c3398f818b153"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Ivanti Sentry CVE-2026-10520 pre-auth command injection POST to /mics/api/v2/sentry/mics-config/handleMessage AIExploitation High
Detects HTTP requests to the unauthenticated Ivanti Sentry MICS endpoint that the public PoC for CVE-2026-10520 abuses. The PoC POSTs a `message=execute+system+/configuration/system/commandexec+<commandexec>…</commandexec>` body to `/mics/api/v2/sentry/mics-config/handleMessage`, the ConfigServiceController route that pipes input straight into OS command execution as root. Rationale: Endpoint path `/mics/api/v2/sentry/mics-config/handleMessage` and the `<commandexec>` payload structure are the exact strings from the public PoC documented by Horizon3, Rapid7 and watchTowr. The endpoint is pre-auth and has no legitimate user-driven traffic, so any external POST is a high-confidence exploit attempt. Defender Advanced Hunting carries no inbound web-request URL telemetry for Ivanti appliances, hence empty `defender_kql`. Datadog/Falcon/CloudWatch left blank because Sentry web access logs don't naturally land in those products. Cross-checked against: • https://horizon3.ai/attack-research/vulnerabilities/cve-2026-10520/ • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/etr-cve-2026-10520-cve-2026-10523-multiple-critical-vulnerabilities-affecting-ivanti-sentry/ • https://labs.watchtowr.com/more-evidence-that-words-dont-mean-what-we-thought-they-meant-ivanti-sentry-pre-auth-os-command-injection-cve-2026-10520/ • https://www.shadowserver.org/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal vulnerability scanners (Tenable Nessus, Rapid7 InsightVM, Qualys) running authenticated CVE-2026-10520 plugin probes
  • Ivanti TAC vendor support running CVE verification scripts against the appliance during a ticket
  • Authorized red-team / pentest engagement targeting the appliance from a known testing subnet
  • Internal change-validation script that hits handleMessage to confirm patch deployment
Suppression filter
and not (cIP in ("<scanner_subnet_1>","<scanner_subnet_2>") or csUserAgent has_any ("Nessus","Qualys","InsightVM","Rapid7"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm src IP is external/untrusted; check if it matches your sanctioned scanner allowlist (Nessus/Qualys/Rapid7 source subnets). Pull the full POST body if your WAF/proxy preserves it and look for `<commandexec>` or `execute+system+/configuration/system/commandexec`. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the perimeter; confirm appliance is at patched version 10.5.2 / 10.6.2 / 10.7.1 — if not, take the admin portal off the internet immediately. 3) Hunt: pivot on the appliance hostname into UC2 (Java→shell post-exploit) for the last 30 days, check `/tmp` and Tomcat webapps dir for new files, and verify no new admin users were added via Sentry console audit logs.
let lookback = 24h;
union isfuzzy=true
  (W3CIISLog
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
   | where csUriStem has "/mics/api/v2/sentry/mics-config/handleMessage" or csUriStem has "mics-config/handleMessage"
   | project TimeGenerated, Source="W3CIISLog", Computer, SrcIP=cIP, Method=csMethod, Uri=csUriStem, Status=scStatus, UserAgent=csUserAgent),
  (CommonSecurityLog
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
   | where RequestURL has "/mics/api/v2/sentry/mics-config/handleMessage" or Message has_any ("mics-config/handleMessage","<commandexec>","execute+system+/configuration/system/commandexec")
   | project TimeGenerated, Source="CommonSecurityLog", Computer=DestinationHostName, SrcIP=SourceIP, Method=RequestMethod, Uri=RequestURL, Status=tostring(EventOutcome), UserAgent=RequestClientApplication),
  (ImWebSession
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
   | where Url has "/mics/api/v2/sentry/mics-config/handleMessage"
   | project TimeGenerated, Source="ImWebSession", Computer=DstHostname, SrcIP=SrcIpAddr, Method=HttpMethod, Uri=Url, Status=tostring(HttpStatusCode), UserAgent=HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ivanti Sentry Tomcat/Java process spawns shell or recon LOLBin as root (CVE-2026-10520 post-exploit) AIInstallation High
Detects the Sentry MICS web daemon (Tomcat-hosted Java) spawning `/bin/sh`, `/bin/bash`, `id`, `whoami`, `curl`, `wget`, `nc`, or interpreters as root — the post-exploitation signature of a successful CVE-2026-10520 OS command injection. Hits both the PoC's `id` smoke test and second-stage tool download. Rationale: Parent `java` running Tomcat (`catalina`, `tomcat`, `mics`, `sentry`, `mifs` in command line) is the Ivanti Sentry MICS web container. Children `/bin/sh`, `id`, `whoami`, `curl`, `wget` as root match both the public PoC's `id` smoke test and the watchTowr-documented second-stage download pattern. Java spawning shell at root on a Linux appliance is essentially never legitimate. CloudWatch left blank because Sentry is an on-prem appliance. Cross-checked against: • https://horizon3.ai/attack-research/vulnerabilities/cve-2026-10520/ • https://labs.watchtowr.com/more-evidence-that-words-dont-mean-what-we-thought-they-meant-ivanti-sentry-pre-auth-os-command-injection-cve-2026-10520/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/06/10/ivanti-sentry-cve-2026-10520-cve-2026-10523/ • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/etr-cve-2026-10520-cve-2026-10523-multiple-critical-vulnerabilities-affecting-ivanti-sentry/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004 T1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Ivanti vendor patch installer that legitimately shells out via the web admin (only during a controlled maintenance window — should be rare)
  • Sentry internal diagnostic command run via the admin UI by an authenticated administrator (`id`/`uname` would be unusual but possible)
  • Custom MDM compliance hook configured by the customer that calls out to a shell script
  • Forensic / DFIR tooling running on the appliance under root during incident response (will spike right after suspected compromise — annotate IR engagements)
Suppression filter
and not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("ivanti-patch","sentry-upgrade","yum update","rpm -U") and ChildCmd has_any ("id","uname"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the `ParentCmd` and `ChildCmd` — if child is `id`/`whoami`/`uname` with no args, it is almost certainly the public PoC's smoke test. Pivot UC1 on the same DeviceName within ±5 minutes to find the inbound POST to `/mics/api/v2/sentry/mics-config/handleMessage` that triggered it. 2) Contain: isolate the appliance from the network immediately (the attacker has root); preserve `/tmp`, Tomcat webapps and logs for forensics; do NOT reboot. 3) Hunt: list new files in `/tmp`, `/var/tmp`, `/opt/mobileiron/`, Tomcat webapps; review outbound network connections from the appliance for the last 30 days; check `/etc/passwd`, cron, systemd units, and SSH `authorized_keys` for persistence; rotate all credentials and certificates the appliance held.
let lookback = 24h;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "java"
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("catalina","tomcat","sentry","mics","mifs","ConfigServiceController")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","id","whoami","curl","wget","uname","nc","ncat","python","python3","perl","busybox","hostname","ip","ifconfig")
| where AccountName =~ "root" or InitiatingProcessAccountName =~ "root"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
let lookback = 24h;
union isfuzzy=true
  (ImProcessCreate
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
   | where ParentProcessName endswith "/java" or ParentProcessName =~ "java"
   | where ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("catalina","tomcat","sentry","mics","mifs","ConfigServiceController")
   | where TargetProcessName has_any ("/sh","/bash","/dash","/id","/whoami","/curl","/wget","/uname","/nc","/ncat","/python","/perl","/busybox","/hostname")
   | where ActorUsername =~ "root"
   | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
             ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine,
             TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine),
  (Syslog
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
   | where SyslogMessage has "type=EXECVE"
   | where SyslogMessage has_any ("/bin/sh","/bin/bash","/usr/bin/id","/usr/bin/whoami","/usr/bin/curl","/usr/bin/wget","/usr/bin/nc","/usr/bin/ncat")
   | where SyslogMessage has_any ("tomcat","catalina","mics","sentry")
   | where SyslogMessage has "uid=0" or SyslogMessage has "auid=0"
   | project TimeGenerated, HostName, Computer, SyslogMessage)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ivanti Sentry instances vulnerable to CVE-2026-10520 / CVE-2026-10523 in software inventory AIExploitation High
Surfaces every onboarded Ivanti Sentry (formerly MobileIron Sentry) appliance whose installed version is below the patched releases (10.5.2 / 10.6.2 / 10.7.1) and therefore vulnerable to the actively-exploited command-injection chain. Use this to drive the BOD 26-04 three-day patch SLA and to prioritise UC1/UC2 alerts. Rationale: Patched versions 10.5.2 / 10.6.2 / 10.7.1 confirmed by Rapid7 and Help Net Security advisories. Joining TVM output against DeviceInfo.IsInternetFacing surfaces the highest-priority assets first — Shadowserver explicitly warned that any unpatched internet-exposed Sentry is likely already compromised. Sigma skipped (inventory-shaped, not a single event). Datadog/Falcon/CloudWatch skipped because vulnerability posture data does not live there. Cross-checked against: • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/etr-cve-2026-10520-cve-2026-10523-multiple-critical-vulnerabilities-affecting-ivanti-sentry/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/06/10/ivanti-sentry-cve-2026-10520-cve-2026-10523/ • https://securityaffairs.com/193530/uncategorized/cve-2026-10520-exploited-ivanti-sentry-gateways-compromised-shortly-after-patch-release.html
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Appliance already decommissioned but still indexed in TVM until next reconciliation
  • Appliance patched in the last 24 hours; TVM scan lag has not yet refreshed the version
  • Recommended-update KB ID populated by a different Ivanti CVE backporting the same code base — confirm CveId matches
  • Custom-built clone of MobileIron sources fingerprinted as `Sentry` by the inventory tool
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull `IsInternetFacing=true` rows first — those are the BOD 26-04 priority. Confirm the version string against vendor's matrix (anything <10.5.2 / <10.6.2 / <10.7.1 is vulnerable). 2) Contain: apply the vendor patch within the three-day CISA SLA; if patching is not possible inside the window, remove the admin portal from internet exposure (firewall rule on TCP/8443 to the MICS interface) per BOD 26-04 guidance. 3) Hunt: for every previously-internet-facing appliance, run UC1 and UC2 retroactively over the last 30 days to determine whether exploitation already occurred before patching — Shadowserver's position is that unpatched-and-exposed = compromised.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where CveId in ("CVE-2026-10520","CVE-2026-10523")
   or (SoftwareVendor in~ ("ivanti","mobileiron") and SoftwareName has_any ("sentry","mobileiron sentry"))

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Outbound traffic to Tchap/Matrix government domains from non-baseline endpoint (breach reuse / phishing-infra check) · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] PowerShell invoked with hardcoded LDAP bind credentials (Tchap leaked-script pattern)
PowerShell invoked with hardcoded LDAP bind credentials (Tchap leaked-script pattern) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts for PowerShell scripts that embed LDAP bind credentials in source — the exact pattern that leaked from the Tchap breach. Targets ConvertTo-SecureString / DirectoryEntry / PSCredential constructions paired with literal password material so analysts can find and rotate exposed scripts in their own estate before they're scraped from a code-sharing channel. Rationale: Article states the threat actor exfiltrated "hardcoded LDAP credentials leaked via a PowerShell script." These specific Win32 PowerShell idioms (LDAP://, DirectoryEntry, ConvertTo-SecureString, PSCredential) are the canonical way LDAP binds are written in PS, and pairing them with literal password keywords filters out interactive Get-Credential calls. Cross-checked against MITRE T1552.001 and SigmaHQ rule pool — no existing rule covers this specific LDAP-bind-with-inline-secret pattern. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1552/001/ • https://github.com/SigmaHQ/sigma/tree/master/rules/windows/process_creation
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1078.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmin migration scripts that legitimately bind to AD with a service account password during a one-off cutover
  • Vendor product installers (SCCM, Exchange setup) that probe schema using DirectorySearcher with prompted creds
  • Identity-tooling vendors (Quest, ManageEngine) shipping PS wrappers that embed -AsPlainText for unattended runs
  • Pentest/red-team training labs running BloodHound or PowerView with sample creds in commandline
  • Backup software (Veeam, Rubrik) using Active Directory connectors with -Force flag during scheduled jobs
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe", "msiexec.exe", "veeam.backup.shell.exe")) | where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Program Files\Microsoft\Exchange Server\", @"\Program Files\Veeam\", @"\Program Files\ManageEngine\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full ProcessCommandLine and the parent process tree — is the script invoked from a known automation account (svc-*, NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM via Task Scheduler) or from an interactive user shell? Check the InitiatingProcessFolderPath for code repositories, shared file servers, or developer home directories where the script likely lives. 2) Contain: if the credential is a real, currently-valid AD bind account, immediately rotate it in AD and revoke active Kerberos tickets for that principal; quarantine the script file on the host. 3) Hunt: pivot on the bind account's sAMAccountName across IdentityLogonEvents / SigninLogs for any non-script logon over the last 30 days, and search file shares (DeviceFileEvents on .ps1/.psm1/.bat) for other copies of the same credential string.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("LDAP://", "DirectoryEntry", "DirectorySearcher", "ConvertTo-SecureString", "PSCredential")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-AsPlainText", "Password", "passwd", "BindDN", "-Force")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\powershell.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\pwsh.exe"
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| where CommandLine has_any ("LDAP://", "DirectoryEntry", "DirectorySearcher", "ConvertTo-SecureString", "PSCredential")
| where CommandLine has_any ("-AsPlainText", "Password", "passwd", "BindDN", "-Force")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: PowerShell With Hardcoded LDAP Bind Credentials
id: 7b3f2c98-6a14-4d22-9b8f-3c2ea7d551e0
description: Detects PowerShell invocations that embed LDAP bind credentials inline (LDAP://, DirectoryEntry, ConvertTo-SecureString, PSCredential) alongside literal password material. Pattern matches the leaked Tchap administrator script.
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/french-govt-says-tchap-breach-affected-over-73-000-accounts/
author: thn-usecases
date: 2026/06/12
tags:
  - attack.credential_access
  - attack.t1552.001
  - attack.t1078.002
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_proc:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
  selection_ldap:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'LDAP://'
      - 'DirectoryEntry'
      - 'DirectorySearcher'
      - 'ConvertTo-SecureString'
      - 'PSCredential'
  selection_secret:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '-AsPlainText'
      - 'Password'
      - 'passwd'
      - 'BindDN'
      - '-Force'
  condition: selection_proc and selection_ldap and selection_secret
falsepositives:
  - Legitimate Active Directory automation scripts using Get-Credential prompts
  - Vendor installers that probe directory schema at setup time
level: medium
source:(windows.sysmon OR windows.security) @EventID:(1 OR 4688) @Image:(*\powershell.exe OR *\PowerShell.exe OR *\POWERSHELL.EXE OR *\pwsh.exe OR *\PWSH.EXE) (@CommandLine:(*LDAP\:\/\/* OR *DirectoryEntry* OR *DirectorySearcher* OR *ConvertTo-SecureString* OR *PSCredential*)) AND (@CommandLine:(*-AsPlainText* OR *Password* OR *passwd* OR *BindDN* OR *-Force*))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ImageFileName=/\\(powershell|pwsh)\.exe$/i
| regex("(LDAP:\\/\\/|DirectoryEntry|DirectorySearcher|ConvertTo-SecureString|PSCredential)", field=CommandLine)
| regex("(-AsPlainText|Password|passwd|BindDN|-Force)", field=CommandLine)
| NOT (UserName=/\$$/)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as cmd from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") (Processes.process="*LDAP://*" OR Processes.process="*DirectoryEntry*" OR Processes.process="*DirectorySearcher*" OR Processes.process="*ConvertTo-SecureString*" OR Processes.process="*PSCredential*") (Processes.process="*-AsPlainText*" OR Processes.process="*Password*" OR Processes.process="*passwd*" OR Processes.process="*BindDN*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where NOT match(user,"\\$$")
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as cmd from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") (Processes.process="*LDAP://*" OR Processes.process="*DirectoryEntry*" OR Processes.process="*DirectorySearcher*" OR Processes.process="*ConvertTo-SecureString*" OR Processes.process="*PSCredential*") (Processes.process="*-AsPlainText*" OR Processes.process="*Password*" OR Processes.process="*passwd*" OR Processes.process="*BindDN*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where NOT match(user,"\\$$")
Outbound traffic to Tchap/Matrix government domains from non-baseline endpoint (breach reuse / phishing-infra check) AICommand & Control Low
Surfaces hosts reaching tchap.gouv.fr or matrix.agent.education.tchap.gouv.fr from estates that don't normally communicate with French government messaging infrastructure. Catches both (a) lookalike phishing domains harvesting credentials post-breach and (b) leaked French-government contractor laptops phoning the legitimate service from unexpected segments. Rationale: Article names the two operational domains (tchap.gouv.fr and matrix.agent.education.tchap.gouv.fr) and notes the actor scraped 13.5GB plus 650K messages — meaning their data-handling infrastructure is now an IOC pivot. For non-French-gov tenants any contact with these hosts from a baseline-new endpoint is worth a look (either a leaked French contractor identity reusing the platform from an unmonitored device, or a typo-squatted phishing host masquerading as Tchap). Anti-join against 90d baseline keeps known-good users out of the alert. Cross-checked against: • https://www.tchap.gouv.fr/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1071/001/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1567
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • New French public-sector contractor onboarded — first legitimate Tchap session from their laptop
  • Security researcher / threat-intel team manually browsing the Tchap web app for indicator confirmation
  • Mobile device synced over corporate Wi-Fi where Matrix client retries after a connectivity flap
  • Reverse-DNS scanner or asset-discovery tool that probes .gouv.fr subdomains as part of a broader sweep
  • User reads the article and clicks the embedded tchap.gouv.fr link from a news site
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("element.exe", "element-desktop.exe", "riot.exe") | where not (InitiatingProcessAccountName has_any ("securityteam", "threat-intel", "soc-"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the DeviceId belongs to a French-government-adjacent user or contractor — check the InitiatingProcessAccountName and HR/CMDB for any France-region tagging, and verify the URL resolves to the genuine Tchap CIDR (not a lookalike). 2) Contain: if the host is NOT expected to talk to French gov infrastructure, isolate via EDR and capture browser history and any Matrix-client credentials cached locally. 3) Hunt: pivot on the InitiatingProcessAccountName across SigninLogs / AADSignInEventsBeta for OAuth grants to Matrix/Element clients in the last 14 days, and search EmailEvents for inbound mail from senders impersonating @tchap.gouv.fr or @dinum.gouv.fr that may have delivered a phishing lure.
let Baseline = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp between (ago(90d) .. ago(7d))
    | where RemoteUrl has_any ("tchap.gouv.fr", "matrix.agent.education.tchap.gouv.fr")
    | summarize by DeviceId;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("tchap.gouv.fr", "matrix.agent.education.tchap.gouv.fr")
| join kind=leftanti Baseline on DeviceId
| summarize FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), ConnectionCount = count(), Urls = make_set(RemoteUrl, 25)
          by DeviceName, DeviceId, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by FirstSeen desc
let Baseline = ImWebSession
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(90d) .. ago(7d))
    | where Url has_any ("tchap.gouv.fr", "matrix.agent.education.tchap.gouv.fr")
    | summarize by SrcHostname;
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has_any ("tchap.gouv.fr", "matrix.agent.education.tchap.gouv.fr")
| join kind=leftanti Baseline on SrcHostname
| summarize FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Hits = count(), Urls = make_set(Url, 25)
          by SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername
| order by FirstSeen desc

Europol Disrupts AudiA6 Crypto Laundering Service Used by Ransomware Gangs

The Hacker News
2026-06-12 12 use cases 5 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Authorities in Europe have disrupted AudiA6, a cryptocurrency laundering service used by ransomware gangs and cybercriminal networks. Europol, in a statement issued Thursday, said the dismantling of AudiA6 cut off a "key financial pipeline used to wash hundreds of millions in illicit profits." The service is estimated to have been used to launder more than €336 million (~$389 million) since the

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] DNS / web egress to AudiA6 money-mule registration infrastructure domains · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
DNS / web egress to AudiA6 money-mule registration infrastructure domains AICommand & Control High
Hunt for hosts in the estate resolving or connecting to the 19 domains Europol/DOJ identified as registration infrastructure for fraudulent KYC accounts on crypto exchanges by the AudiA6 laundering service. A workstation resolving these is a strong indicator of money-mule activity, insider account-opening fraud, or compromised user enrolling in the laundering ring. Rationale: All 19 domains are explicitly named in the DOJ/Europol disclosure as infrastructure the AudiA6 operators registered and controlled to create mule accounts on crypto exchanges. They are not generic infra — any internal host resolving them post-disclosure is anomalous. Cross-checked the article body and the named ToHN domain list against the DOJ press release for the AudiA6 indictment. Cross-checked against: • https://www.europol.europa.eu/media-press/newsroom • https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr
ATT&CKT1583.001 T1568
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Web.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat intel analyst manually browsing the seized domain banners after takedown
  • Email gateway / URL sandbox detonating the domains for analysis
  • Marketing/MarTech team evaluating a legit deliverability vendor that shares a name (e.g. a real 'postify' or 'inboxally' SaaS)
  • DNS sinkhole / passive-DNS aggregators replaying historical queries
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","SenseIR.exe","smartscreen.exe","MpCmdRun.exe","DefenderDlpComp.exe")
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe") and AccountName in~ ("threatintel","soc-analyst"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pivot on the source host and user — pull the process context (browser, mail client, scripting host?) that issued the resolution and whether the connection completed (HTTP/TLS to the resolved IP). Check if the user has crypto-exchange accounts via DLP/UEBA. 2) Contain: block all 19 domains and their resolved IPs at the proxy/DNS firewall; force-reset the user's exchange-portal sessions if any are detected; quarantine the host if outbound POSTs to exchange KYC endpoints followed the lookup. 3) Hunt: search 90d back across DNS/proxy for any of the 19 domains; pivot on the resolved IPs to find sibling infra; look for HR/insider-risk signals (recent identity-document scans, ID photos uploaded, payroll changes); check email for inbound recruiter messages in Russian referencing 'crypto work' or 'KYC verification'.
let MuleDomains = dynamic(["designli.pictures","pheontx.eu","smplfy.in","sumato-soft.org","technobrains.dev","lett.email","trayo.app","deliverly.top","inboxly.top","postfast.eu","postino.click","inboxally.agency","mailora.eu","postify.email","quix.express","flowcomm.click","qube.black","deliverlett.com","lettermail.eu"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
| extend Host = tolower(tostring(split(RemoteUrl, "/")[0]))
| where Host has_any (MuleDomains)
   or RemoteUrl has_any (MuleDomains)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, Host
| order by Timestamp desc
let MuleDomains = dynamic(["designli.pictures","pheontx.eu","smplfy.in","sumato-soft.org","technobrains.dev","lett.email","trayo.app","deliverly.top","inboxly.top","postfast.eu","postino.click","inboxally.agency","mailora.eu","postify.email","quix.express","flowcomm.click","qube.black","deliverlett.com","lettermail.eu"]);
let DnsHits = union isfuzzy=true
    (ImDnsActivity
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
        | where DnsQuery has_any (MuleDomains)
        | project TimeGenerated, Host=DvcHostname, SrcHost=SrcHostname, SrcIp=SrcIpAddr, Query=DnsQuery, Source="ImDnsActivity"),
    (DnsEvents
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
        | where Name has_any (MuleDomains)
        | project TimeGenerated, Host=Computer, SrcHost=Computer, SrcIp=ClientIP, Query=Name, Source="DnsEvents");
let WebHits = union isfuzzy=true
    (CommonSecurityLog
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
        | where DestinationHostName has_any (MuleDomains) or RequestURL has_any (MuleDomains)
        | project TimeGenerated, Host=SourceHostName, SrcHost=SourceHostName, SrcIp=SourceIP, Query=coalesce(DestinationHostName, RequestURL), Source="CommonSecurityLog"),
    (ImWebSession
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
        | where HttpHostName has_any (MuleDomains) or Url has_any (MuleDomains)
        | project TimeGenerated, Host=DvcHostname, SrcHost=SrcHostname, SrcIp=SrcIpAddr, Query=coalesce(HttpHostName, Url), Source="ImWebSession");
union DnsHits, WebHits
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Hits=count(), Queries=make_set(Query, 25), Sources=make_set(Source) by Host, SrcIp
| order by LastSeen desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium

| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT

| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200

The ShinyHunters extortion crew exploited an unpatched flaw in Oracle PeopleSoft to break into enterprise systems, steal data, and demand payment to keep it private. The campaign hit universities hardest. Google's Mandiant attributes it to the group it tracks as UNC6240, and dates the activity between May 27 and June 9. Oracle did not publish its advisory until June 10, so the bug was a

Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] UNC6240/ShinyHunters C2 — Connections to azurenetfiles.net or Mandiant-Listed Staging IPs · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Outbound SMB from PeopleSoft Host to Public IP (NetNTLM Coercion) · [LLM] ShinyHunters Extortion Marker File Drop — README-IF-YOU-SEE-THIS-YOUVE-BEEN-HACKED.TXT · [LLM] UNC6240 Lateral SSH Fanout Script (*_fanout.sh) Creation or Execution · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Oracle PeopleSoft PSEMHUB CVE-2026-35273 Exploitation Attempt AIExploitation Medium
Detects unauthenticated external HTTP POST requests against the Environment Management Hub (/PSEMHUB/hub) and Integration Broker listener (/PSIGW/HttpListeningConnector) — the two entry points Oracle confirmed for the ShinyHunters/UNC6240 zero-day. Normal user sessions do not POST to these endpoints, so external traffic here is the primary exploit signal. Rationale: Article body explicitly names /PSEMHUB/hub and /PSIGW/HttpListeningConnector as the only endpoints Oracle recommends blocking — exploitation MUST traverse one of them. Mandiant's hunt guidance also called out external POSTs to these exact paths in WebLogic access logs.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal PeopleSoft administrators using PSEMHUB management UI from outside the org via VPN that egresses public IP
  • Synthetic monitoring or vendor uptime probes hitting /PSEMHUB endpoints
  • Pen-testers running PeopleSoft assessment scans
  • Misconfigured load balancers double-NATing internal traffic to appear external
Suppression filter
| where csUserAgent !has_any ("Pingdom", "UptimeRobot", "StatusCake", "Datadog Synthetics")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full HTTP request body and User-Agent for the offending source IP from raw IIS/WebLogic logs and check status code — 200/302 means likely successful exploit. Cross-reference source IP against the article's staging IPs (142.11.200.186-190, 108.174.202.99, 176.120.22.24). 2) Contain: block /PSEMHUB/* and /PSIGW/HttpListeningConnector at the perimeter WAF/firewall immediately (Oracle-approved mitigation). Disable PSEMHUB service on multi-server installs; remove the PSEMHUB application on single-server installs. 3) Hunt: on the targeted PeopleSoft host, run UC2/UC3 queries for .jsp webshells under PSEMHUB.war and XML changes under envmetadata/data/environment within ±2 hours of the POST.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csMethod =~ "POST"
| where csUriStem has_any ("/PSEMHUB/hub", "/PSEMHUB/", "/PSIGW/HttpListeningConnector")
| where not(ipv4_is_private(cIP))
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, sSiteName, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, csUserAgent, scStatus, scBytes, csBytes
| order by TimeGenerated desc

PeopleSoft Webshell — .jsp Created Under PSEMHUB.war AIInstallation High
Detects creation or modification of .jsp files inside the PSEMHUB.war web application directory — Mandiant's hunt guidance calls this out as the post-exploit webshell drop point for CVE-2026-35273. Legitimate PSEMHUB deployments do not write new JSPs at runtime. Rationale: Article quotes Mandiant directly: 'Unexpected .jsp files under the PSEMHUB.war web application directory'. The path is a unique deployment artifact of PSEMHUB; any .jsp written outside a planned deploy is exploitation evidence.
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate PeopleTools patch deployment via Oracle Universal Installer rewriting .war contents
  • Application server restart redeploying PSEMHUB.war from staged build
  • Vendor consultant performing in-place PSEMHUB customization
  • Backup/restore operation extracting .war contents to original path
Response runbook
1) Triage: hash the new .jsp and compare against PSEMHUB.war manifest from Oracle (envtools README ships an inventory). Read first 200 lines of the file — exploit drops are typically <2KB and contain Runtime.getRuntime().exec / ProcessBuilder. 2) Contain: kill the WebLogic JVM hosting PSEMHUB.war (java.exe / weblogic process), delete the .jsp, and apply the perimeter block from UC1. Preserve a forensic copy first (cp before rm). 3) Hunt: walk InitiatingProcessId chain backwards to find the originating HTTP exploit request in IIS/WebLogic access logs; pivot to UC3 (XMLDecoder XML modifications) and UC5 (egress to azurenetfiles.net) on same host within last 14d.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified", "FileRenamed")
| where FileName endswith ".jsp"
| where FolderPath has_any ("PSEMHUB.war", @"\PSEMHUB\", "/PSEMHUB/")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msiexec.exe", "ant.exe", "jar.exe", "tar.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, FileSize,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessAccountDomain
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified")
| where TargetFileExtension =~ "jsp"
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("PSEMHUB.war", @"\PSEMHUB\", "/PSEMHUB/")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("msiexec.exe", "ant.exe", "jar.exe", "tar.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

PeopleSoft XMLDecoder Persistence via envmetadata/data/environment .xml Modification AIInstallation High
Detects modification of .xml files under the PeopleTools envmetadata/data/environment path — Mandiant warned this is the XMLDecoder deserialization persistence vector that fires on the next PSEMHUB restart. Legitimate environment XML changes occur only during planned PeopleTools upgrades. Rationale: Article quote: 'Recently changed .xml files under the web doc root's envmetadata/data/environment, which can be abused for XMLDecoder persistence that fires on the next restart.' This is a uniquely-named PeopleTools subtree — writes by a non-installer process are anomalous.
ATT&CKT1547 T1505
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Scheduled PeopleTools application server bounce that legitimately rewrites environment XML
  • DBA running EnvMetadata refresh during change window
  • Oracle Universal Installer applying PSEMHUB CPU patch
  • PeopleTools 8.61→8.62 in-place upgrade
  • Backup tooling restoring envmetadata directory after rollback
Response runbook
1) Triage: diff the modified XML against the last-known-good copy from your config-management backup. Look for <java> tags, <object class="java.lang.ProcessBuilder">, or base64-encoded blobs — XMLDecoder gadget signatures. Pull the InitiatingProcess details to confirm if it's a known patch tool. 2) Contain: do NOT restart the PSEMHUB / app server until the XML is verified clean — restart is the trigger. Replace the .xml from backup, snapshot the host for forensics, then bounce. 3) Hunt: scan for other XMLDecoder gadget artefacts (.jsp drops from UC2) on this host and across the PeopleSoft cluster; pivot on InitiatingProcessId to find the parent shell.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified", "FileRenamed")
| where FileName endswith ".xml"
| where FolderPath has_any ("envmetadata/data/environment", @"envmetadata\data\environment")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("psadmin.exe", "setup.exe", "psemagent.exe", "pscbl.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, FileSize,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified")
| where TargetFileExtension =~ "xml"
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("envmetadata/data/environment", @"envmetadata\data\environment")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("psadmin.exe", "setup.exe", "psemagent.exe", "pscbl.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Outbound SMB from PeopleSoft Host to Public IP (NetNTLM Coercion) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects TCP/445 connections from PeopleSoft/WebLogic hosts to public IPs — Mandiant's CVE-2026-35273 advisory calls this out as the NetNTLM hash-capture chain the exploit leverages against the application server's machine account. Production PeopleSoft hosts should never SMB to the internet. Rationale: Article quote: 'Outbound SMB traffic on port 445 from PeopleSoft hosts to external destinations, which the exploit chain may use to capture machine-account NetNTLM hashes.' Public-bound 445 from a server-class host is a near-perfect signal — internet SMB has no legitimate use case for an enterprise PeopleSoft instance.
ATT&CKT1187 T1557
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Misconfigured Azure Files / O365 SharePoint share mount targeting public DNS
  • Backup product replicating to a cloud SMB endpoint
  • Developer testing SMB to a Tailscale/ZeroTier exit node
  • Network probe / vulnerability scanner originating from PeopleSoft host
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("backupagent.exe", "veeam.backup.shell.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the destination IP and check against the article's staging IPs (142.11.200.186-190, 108.174.202.99, 176.120.22.24) and threat intel for SMB-coercion C2 (Responder, Inveigh, NTLM relay infrastructure). Identify the initiating process — anything that isn't svchost/lsass is suspicious. 2) Contain: block TCP/445 egress at the perimeter for the PeopleSoft VLAN immediately (no legitimate use case). Force the machine account to rotate its password. 3) Hunt: search SigninLogs / IdentityLogonEvents for the machine account ($-suffixed) authenticating from unexpected sources in the last 30 days, indicating relayed/cracked hash use.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where RemotePort == 445
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where ActionType in ("ConnectionSuccess", "ConnectionAttempt")
| lookup kind=inner DeviceInfo on DeviceId
| where DeviceName has_any ("psem", "psft", "peoplesoft", "pshr", "psfs", "psoft") or LoggedOnUsers has_any ("psadm", "psemagent")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, LocalPort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where DstPortNumber == 445
| where NetworkProtocol =~ "TCP"
| where not(ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr))
| where DvcHostname has_any ("psem", "psft", "peoplesoft", "pshr", "psfs")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkBytes, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

UNC6240/ShinyHunters C2 — Connections to azurenetfiles.net or Mandiant-Listed Staging IPs AICommand & Control Medium
Detects DNS resolution or direct network connections to the MeshCentral C2 domain azurenetfiles.net (typo-squat of Azure NetApp Files) and to the five sequential Python SimpleHTTP staging hosts (142.11.200.186-190) plus the two additional Mandiant-attributed IPs. These are hard IOCs from the active campaign. Rationale: Article-supplied IOCs: azurenetfiles.net was the C2 server for MeshCentral agents disguised as Azure binaries; 142.11.200.186-190 were five sequential Python SimpleHTTP servers exposing the attacker's open directories (Mandiant triaged them). 108.174.202.99 and 176.120.22.24 are the other Mandiant-attributed staging IPs. Atomic IOCs with no legitimate business use.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1219 T1568
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal sandbox/researcher detonating samples and resolving these IOCs deliberately
  • Threat-intel platform passively beaconing IOC lists for verification
  • Honeypot or deception infrastructure intentionally contacting attacker IPs
  • Tabletop / purple-team exercise replaying the campaign
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("cape.exe", "cuckoo.exe", "any.run-agent.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the source host and the process making the connection (InitiatingProcessFileName). Confirm it's not a sandbox / TI tool. Check the process — MeshCentral agents typically appear as 'msh.exe' or named like Microsoft Azure binaries (per article). 2) Contain: isolate the device immediately via Defender/EDR network isolation. Sinkhole azurenetfiles.net at DNS and add IPs to perimeter blocklist. Rotate credentials for users who logged on to the affected host in the last 14d. 3) Hunt: pivot on InitiatingProcessFileName/SHA256 to find other hosts running the same MeshCentral agent; review autoruns / services on each for persistence. Cross-check against UC1/UC2/UC3 PeopleSoft exploit indicators.
let IOC_IPs = dynamic(["142.11.200.186","142.11.200.187","142.11.200.188","142.11.200.189","142.11.200.190","108.174.202.99","176.120.22.24"]);
let IOC_Domain = "azurenetfiles.net";
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in (IOC_IPs)
   or RemoteUrl has IOC_Domain
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| union (
    DeviceEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where ActionType == "DnsQueryResponse"
    | where AdditionalFields has IOC_Domain or RemoteUrl has IOC_Domain
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
  )
| order by Timestamp desc
let IOC_IPs = dynamic(["142.11.200.186","142.11.200.187","142.11.200.188","142.11.200.189","142.11.200.190","108.174.202.99","176.120.22.24"]);
let IOC_Domain = "azurenetfiles.net";
(union isfuzzy=true
  (ImNetworkSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where DstIpAddr in (IOC_IPs) or DstHostname has IOC_Domain or Url has IOC_Domain
    | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, DstHostname, Url),
  (ImDnsActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where DnsQuery has IOC_Domain or DstIpAddr in (IOC_IPs)
    | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DnsQuery, DstIpAddr))
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ShinyHunters Extortion Marker File Drop — README-IF-YOU-SEE-THIS-YOUVE-BEEN-HACKED.TXT AIActions on Objectives High
Detects creation of the verbatim ShinyHunters/UNC6240 marker file written by the [victim]_fanout.sh lateral-movement script into PeopleSoft directories. The exact filename is the highest-fidelity post-compromise IOC in this campaign. Rationale: Article quote: 'drops a marker file named README-IF-YOU-SEE-THIS-YOUVE-BEEN-HACKED.TXT into PeopleSoft directories.' The literal filename is unique enough to detect with zero false-positive risk outside of threat-intel sharing.
ATT&CKT1657 T1485
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security team running tabletop / purple-team exercise replaying the IOC
  • Threat-intel artefact accidentally extracted from a sample-sharing platform
  • Researcher writing a write-up of the campaign on a research VM
  • Incident-response archive containing prior evidence being unpacked
  • Detection-engineering test of this rule
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the file is the real marker (compare contents — should reference ShinyHunters leak site). Identify InitiatingProcess — likely bash/sh executing *_fanout.sh, or a shell child of WebLogic. The file location tells you which PeopleSoft directory was hit (envmetadata, doc root, etc.). 2) Contain: isolate the host immediately. Treat the breach as confirmed — preserve volatile state (memory, /tmp, bash_history) before reboot. Notify legal/comms for breach-disclosure clock. 3) Hunt: enumerate every host in /etc/hosts of the compromised box (that's the fanout target list per the article); query each for the same marker file. Pull bash_history off each — UC4 SMB egress and UC5 C2 IOCs are likely co-present.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "README-IF-YOU-SEE-THIS-YOUVE-BEEN-HACKED.TXT"
   or FileName startswith "README-IF-YOU-SEE-THIS-YOUVE-BEEN-HACKED"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "README-IF-YOU-SEE-THIS-YOUVE-BEEN-HACKED.TXT"
   or TargetFileName startswith "README-IF-YOU-SEE-THIS-YOUVE-BEEN-HACKED"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

UNC6240 Lateral SSH Fanout Script (*_fanout.sh) Creation or Execution AIActions on Objectives High
Detects creation or execution of the shell script the attackers used to spray hardcoded credentials over SSH against internal hosts pulled from /etc/hosts on the compromised PeopleSoft server. The naming convention [victim]_fanout.sh is a hard IOC from Mandiant's triage of the exposed staging directory. Rationale: Article quote: 'The script, named [victim]_fanout.sh, spreads over SSH by spraying a hardcoded list of usernames and passwords against internal hosts pulled from /etc/hosts'. The naming pattern is a direct artefact recovered from Mandiant's open-directory triage on the attacker's port 8888 SimpleHTTP servers.
ATT&CKT1110.001 T1021.004 T1570
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate sysadmin / DevOps tooling using *_fanout.sh naming convention for parallel SSH (e.g. pdsh wrapper) — exclude by repo path
  • SRE chaos-testing scripts using the same suffix
  • Ansible/Salt deployment scripts named *_fanout.sh in a CMDB
  • Red-team / pentester replica of the IOC for control validation
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath !has_any ("/opt/ansible", "/srv/salt", "/var/lib/awx")
Response runbook
1) Triage: cat the script contents — confirm it parses /etc/hosts and iterates SSH attempts with a hardcoded credential list. Pull the file's SHA256 and submit to TI. Identify the parent process (likely WebLogic / java shell-out) for the kill chain. 2) Contain: isolate the host. Reset all SSH credentials present in the script's hardcoded list across the environment immediately. Add the SHA256 to allow/deny lists. 3) Hunt: read /etc/hosts on the affected box — every entry is a potential next target. Query SSH auth logs (Syslog / auditd USER_AUTH) on those hosts for failed-then-successful auth from the compromised PeopleSoft IP in the last 14 days; cross-check for UC6 marker file drops.
(DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified")
| where FileName matches regex @"(?i).+_fanout\.sh$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName)
| union (
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i).+_fanout\.sh"
   or FileName matches regex @"(?i).+_fanout\.sh$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, AccountName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine)
| order by Timestamp desc
(ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified")
| where TargetFileName matches regex @"(?i).+_fanout\.sh$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActorUsername)
| union (
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i).+_fanout\.sh"
   or TargetProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i).+_fanout\.sh"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
